L108: ## Which apps require a review?
L109: 
L110: If you are building an app that can be installed and used by any customer on Intercom, and will have access to their workspace data, you are building a public app. This means that the Intercom team must review and approve your app before it is available to install.
L111: 
L112: Private apps that only access your own paid workspace data do not require a review. You can ignore the rest of this page!
L113: ## Listed vs Unlisted?
L114: 
L115: Your public app has the option of being cite23†listed or cite24†unlisted .
L116: 
L117: ### Listed apps
L118: 
L119: A listed app will be available for anyone to discover and install in the cite5†Intercom App Store†www.intercom.com .
L120: 
L121: This requires filling out the App Listing and App Partner Program pages in the Developer Hub and ensuring that all the requirements for each are met. Read more in the cite16†listing your app guide.
L196: It is better to show too much of your app than not enough. If you do not show all of the functionality of your app as well as the OAuth processes, you will have to resubmit your video.
L197: 
L198: Click "Submit for Review" to submit your app to our team.
L199: 
L200: If you need to discard any changes that have been made to your app to start over, you can use the Discard Changes button on this page.
L201: 
L202: cite39†Image: Discard Changes L203: ## The review process
L204: 
L205: Once your app is with the Intercom team, we will review it to ensure it meets our requirements.
L206: 
L207: You will see a yellow banner at the top of the screen stating it can take up to seven business days for review.
L208: ### Communicating with the Intercom team
L209: 
L210: Our team will reach back out to you in an in-app conversation in the Messenger (find it at the bottom right of any Intercom pages you visit) to let you know about any changes that need to be made to your app. Feel free to ask any questions in that conversation.
L211: 
L212: If you are asked to make changes, you may resubmit your app after making the requested changes and our team will review it further.
L213: 
L214: cite40†Image: Intercom L215: ### Your application's status and visibility
L216: 
L217: During this process, your app will be private and can only be used by you and your team.
L218: 
L219: When your app is approved, it will become a public unlisted app.
L220: 
L221: You'll see the following green banner and blue pill:
L222: 
L223: cite41†Image: Review blurred L224: 
L225: Why is my app unlisted?
L226: We allow your app to be public but unlisted so that you don't necessarily have to set the listing live straight away. You can instead test out your app in a separate staging environment, or send to your customers individually to collect feedback (ie. when in beta).
L227: 
L228: When you want to set your listing live for public installs via the App Store, you will need to select the List in App store option on the App Store listing page.
L229: 
L230: cite42†Image: App store L231: ## Updating your app
L232: 
L233: You may need to make changes to the current details about your app in the review, listing, or OAuth pages. There are two different systems depending on whether this is due to a rejected application or an approved application.
L234: ### Changing a rejected application
L235: 
L236: If your app is rejected, you will need to resubmit your app after you have made the changes that our team has requested.
L237: 
L238: We'll show you exactly where the issue is on the given page, under the header Feedback from Intercom. You can also ask use any questions you may have about the changes in the in-app conversation in the Messenger with our team.
L239: 
L240: cite43†Image: Review L241: Your application can take up to seven business days to review, so ensure everything is fixed. You can then resubmit via the Submit for Review button.
L242: ### Changing an approved application
L243: 
L244: Once your app is approved you are ready to publish. However, if you need to make any changes in the future the app will need to be re-approved by the Intercom team.
L245: 
L246: In the approval flow before your app was published, your app remained in a private state until the team approved it. However, in cases where an app is updated after it is approved and published, the app will remain public with the current functionality until your updates have been approved.
L247: You can see and review all the changes in the Review changes tab in your Developer Hub before you submit again.
L248: 
L249: cite44†Image: Review L250: 
L251: You can also see the changes to the listing being reviewed in your Pending configuration tab, and what's currently visible on the App store in the Approved configuration tab. These can be found on your App store listing page.
L252: 
L253: cite45†Image: App store L254: ## Further app development
L255: 
L256: Once your app has been approved, you may want to continue iterating and developing without touching your production app.
L257: 
L258: We recommend cite46†creating a new app†app.intercom.io on the Developer Hub home page if you haven't already, which can be used purely as a staging app for development purposes. You can populate this with all the URLs and settings for development.
L259: 
L260: What's best practice to prevent editing my production app?
L261: A good rule is to name the development app the same as your production app but append something such as `[Staging]` or `[Dev]` at the end to differentiate these. You'll also see that the production app will be labeled as `Public` and your development app will be labeled as `Private`.

These API resources can be accessed by navigating to the cite4†APIs section of HubSpot’s developer documentation, then drilling down into the specific API you need (e.g., the cite5†contacts API guide or the cite6†retrieve contacts reference page ).

L41: App scope types
L42: 
L43: When you specify the scopes within the `auth` property of your `app-hsmeta.json` cite9†configuration file , there are three different scope types available for you to configure. You must specify the scopes your app will require for installation, but you can also specify two other scope types: conditionally required scopes and optional scopes.
L44:   * Required scopes: scopes that must be authorized by the user and must be present in the `scope` query parameter in your app’s install URL for successful installation. Apps configured with cite10†static auth can only define required scopes.
L45: If your app uses cite11†OAuth authentication , you can also specify conditionally required scopes and optional scopes, which provide more flexibility and control for the permissions that users grant to your app.
L46:   * Conditionally required scopes: scopes that must be authorized by the user only if they’re present in the `scope` query parameter in your app’s install URL for successful installation.
L47:     * This scope type allows you to be flexible and provide a separate install URL for tiered features or scopes that are only required when users enable certain features in your app. For example, you could offer two install URLs to your users: one install URL could include the conditionally required scope in the `scope` query parameter for users with access to a feature, while another install URL omits that scope in the `scope` query parameter for users without access.
L48:     * If a conditionally required scope is present in your app install URL and a user without access to the associated feature attempts to install your app using that URL, the installation will fail.
L49:   * Optional scopes: scopes that are not required to successfully install your app. These scopes are included in the `optional_scope` query parameter in your app’s install URL. For example, if you want your app to be able to fetch cite12†custom object data (which is only available to Enterprise HubSpot accounts), you could add the `crm.objects.custom.read` scope as an optional scope.
L50: Then, when a user attempts to install your app, they’ll be prompted with the optional scopes you specified, and can customize and confirm each optional permission they grant to your app.

L116: # OAuth 2.0
L117: 
L118: OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol that authorizes a client application (like a third-party app) to access specific resources on behalf of a user, without sharing the user’s password. It’s widely used for APIs that need secure, delegated access.
L119: 
L120: HighLevel supports the Authorization Code Grant flow with v2 APIs. Below is the step-by-step procedure to understand and use the OAuth 2.0 flow.
L121: 
L122: * * *
L133:      * Who can install: Who should be able to view and install the app from the Marketplace UI? The recommended setting is `“Both Agency & Sub-account”` to ensure maximum visibility and adoption of your app. However, if you’re building a fully white-labeled SaaS feature intended to be exclusively discovered and installed by agencies for use within their sub-accounts, you may choose to limit visibility to Agencies only.
L134:      * Listing Type: White-label recommended for marketing agencies.
L135: cite64†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L136:   4. After creating the APP you will be taken to the Profile section where you will need to add the details related to your APP. For eg; APP Logo, category, Company Name, APP Description, preview images etc.
L137:   5. After completing the profile details, please click on the Advanced Settings drop down available in the left pane and go to the auth section.
L138:   6. The Auth page will appear as shown in the screenshot below. This is where you’ll configure essential settings for your app’s OAuth integration, including scopes, redirect URLs, and client credentials.
L139: cite65†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L140: 
L141:   * Scopes: Scopes define the level of access your app will have — what data it can read or what actions it can perform on behalf of the user. cite6†Click Here to find all the available Scopes.
L142:     * It’s best practice to request the minimum number of scopes necessary for your app to function.
L143:     * Click on the "Select Scope" dropdown and choose the relevant scopes based on your app’s functionality.
L144:   * Redirect URL: A Redirect URL (also known as a Callback URL) is the destination where the authorization server will send the authorization code after the user installs the app.
L145:     * Enter your redirect URL in the Redirect URL field.
L146:     * Click the "Add" button to save it.
L147:   * Client Keys (ID & Secret): In the Client Keys section:
L148: 
L149:     * Click the "Add" button.
L150:     * Provide a name for your client key pair.
L151:     * Upon saving, your Client ID and Client Secret will be generated.
L152: 
L153: These credentials are used to identify and authenticate your application with the OAuth server during token exchange.
L154: Important: Be sure to copy and securely store your Client Secret immediately. After clicking "OK", you will not be able to view or copy the secret again from the UI.
L155: 
L156: * * *
L157: ## 2. Add the App to Your Desired Locationcite66†​ L158: 
L159:   * Have the location/agency admin visit your Installation URL.
L160:   * Select the location to connect.
L161:   * Redirected to your Redirect URL with an Authorization Code.
L162:   * Exchange the code for an Access Token via the OAuth 2.0 cite67†Get Access Token API.
L163:   * Use the Access Token to call APIs.
L164: 
L165: * * *
L166: ## 3. Get the Installation URLcite68†​ L167: 
L168: Inside your APP Auth Pane available inside the Advanced Settings Section you will be able to see the Install Link at the top of the Page.
L169: 
L170: cite69†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L171: 
L172: Click on the Show button and you will be able to see the Installation URLs which you will be using to install the APP.
L173: 
L174: cite70†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L175: Depending on your usecase and account setup you can either use the standard or the whitelabel version of the Installation URL.
L176: 
L177: Refer to the below steps to install the APP:
L178: 
L179:   1. Copy the Installation URL and open it in your browser.
L180:   2. In case you are not logged in to your GHL account it will ask you to login to your account.

L184:   * In case you are logged in it will show a page showcasing the accounts.

L186: cite72†Image: drawing†storage.googleapis.com L187:   3. Select the account you want to install the APP in.
L188:   4. When a user grants access, their browser is redirected to the specified redirect URI, and the Authorization Code is passed inside the code query parameter.
L189: 
L190:     `
L191: 
L192:     https://myapp.com/oauth/callback/highlevel?code=7676cjcbdc6t76cdcbkjcd09821jknnkj
L193: 
L194:     `
L195: This URL demonstrates a typical OAuth callback scenario for a HighLevel integration. The `code` parameter included in the query string is essential for completing the authorization flow.
L196: 
L197: * * *
L198: ## 4. Listening to Webhook Eventscite73†​ L199: 
L200: The HighLevel Marketplace App allows you to listen to various webhook events, enabling real-time updates and integrations based on user actions.
L201: 
L202: To set up webhook listeners:
L203:   1. Navigate to your app in the Marketplace dashboard.
L204:   2. Click on the "Advanced Settings" dropdown in the left-hand panel.
L205:   3. Go to the "Webhooks" section.
L206:   4. In the input box at the top, enter your webhook URL.
L207:   5. Use the toggle switches next to each event to subscribe to the events you wish to listen for.
L208: 
L209: For a full list of supported webhook events and example payloads, please refer to the documentation: cite61†Webhook Events & Payloads --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L67: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides a standardized interface that allows any compatible AI model or agent to access your Linear data in a simple and secure way.
L68: 
L69: Connect to our MCP server natively in Claude, Cursor, and other clients or use the cite35†`mcp-remote`†github.com module for backwards compatibility with clients that do not support remote MCP.
L70: Linear’s MCP server follows the authenticated remote cite36†MCP spec†modelcontextprotocol.io , so the server is centrally hosted and managed. The Linear MCP server has tools available for finding, creating, and updating objects in Linear like issues, projects, and comments — with more functionality on the way, and cite32†feedback on its functionality is welcomed.
L71: 
L72: For help getting started after setup, see some of our cite37†example prompts .
L73: ## Setupcite38†⁠ L74: ### Generalcite39†⁠ L75: 
L76: Our MCP server uses Streamable HTTP as the primary transport, accessible at the following address. The interactive setup flow uses OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration. You can also authenticate directly with a bearer token or Linear API key — see the FAQ for details.
L77: 
L78: Read-write access is provided through `https://mcp.linear.app/mcp` by default.
L79: 
L80: For read-only access, you have two options:
L81:   * Connect to `https://mcp.linear.app/mcp/readonly`, which only ever exposes read tools.
L82:   * Use the standard `/mcp` endpoint, but only request the `read` OAuth scope. Clients that request `read` are granted read-only access, and the underlying token can’t reach write APIs.
L83: 
L84: For instructions for specific clients, read on. Dedicated setup pages are also available for cite40†Claude , cite41†Cursor , cite42†VS Code , cite43†Windsurf , and cite44†Zed .

L0: # Model Context Protocol (MCP)
L1: 
L2: Let your AI agents interact with the Stripe API by using our MCP server.
L3: 
L4: Read this page in your terminal: [install the Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/install) (v1.43.3+) and run `stripe docs`. [Reference](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/docs)
L5: ## Start here: Integrate with Stripe using skills and plugins
L6: 
L7: Stripe provides skills and plugins for agents to build faster and more accurately. See [Agent skills](https://docs.stripe.com/skills.md) for more information.
L8: 
L9: **Quickstart**: Install the Stripe CLI with `npm install -g @stripe/cli` and run `stripe agent setup`.
L10: The Stripe Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides tools that AI agents can use to interact with the Stripe API and search Stripe’s knowledge base, including documentation and support articles.
L11: ## Set up Stripe MCP with a plugin  (Recommended)
L12: 
L13: [Agent plugins](https://docs.stripe.com/agents/plugin.md) for Stripe automatically configure the Stripe MCP server, install our [skills](https://docs.stripe.com/skills.md), and make sure they’re up-to-date. You get our latest capabilities without configuration or maintenance.
L14: 
L15: To install, run:
L16: 
L17: ```bash
L18: npm install -g @stripe/cli@latest
L19: stripe agent setup
L20: ```
L21: 
L22: This command automatically detects which agents you use, and runs the applicable commands.
L23: ## Manually set up Stripe MCP
L24: 
L25: If your MCP client doesn’t support [agent plugins](https://docs.stripe.com/agents/plugin.md) for Stripe, or you prefer to configure the Stripe MCP server and install the skills manually, follow these instructions:
L26: #### Cursor
L27: 
L28: [Install in Cursor](cursor://anysphere.cursor-deeplink/mcp/install?name=stripe&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL21jcC5zdHJpcGUuY29tIn0%3D)
L29: 
L30: Select **Install in Cursor** to open Cursor and add the Stripe MCP server. To configure it manually, add the following configuration to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`.
L31: 
L32: For more information, see [Cursor’s MCP documentation](https://docs.cursor.com/context/model-context-protocol).
L33: ```json
L34: {
L35:  "mcpServers": {
L36:    "stripe": {
L37:      "url": "https://mcp.stripe.com"
L38:    }
L39:  }
L40: }
L41: ```
L42: #### Claude Code
L43: 
L44: Run the following command to add the Stripe MCP server to Claude Code:
L45: 
L46: ```bash
L47: claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com/
L48: ```
L49: 
L50: After you add the server, authenticate Stripe with OAuth.
L51: 
L52: ```bash
L53: claude /mcp
L54: ```
L55: 
L56: To authenticate with a restricted API key instead of OAuth, use the `--header` option:
L57: 
L58: ```bash
L59: claude mcp add --transport http stripe https://mcp.stripe.com/ --header 'Authorization: Bearer <<YOUR_SECRET_KEY>>'
L60: ```

L314: ## Confirm actions by agents acting on your behalf
L315: 
L316: When you connect an AI agent to Stripe through the MCP server using your user credentials, you authorize the agent to access data and take actions in Stripe on your behalf.
L317: To prevent agents from making mistakes, Stripe requires human confirmation before it takes certain `stripe_api_write` actions, such as refunds and outbound payments. To confirm an action, click the URL provided by your agent and review the details of the request.
L318: ![Confirm a refund request](https://b.stripecdn.com/docs-statics-srv/assets/human-confirmation.d768e677a3bf87585ee29a003df41b00.png)
L319: 
L320: Confirm a refund request
L321: When you click **Approve**, Stripe provides the agent with an approval token, but you need to tell the agent to retry the operation, which doesn’t require human confirmation. If you don’t approve the action within 24 hours, it expires.
L322: ## Use MCP with connected accounts
L323: 
L324: By default, Stripe MCP tools operate on the Stripe account associated with your OAuth session or API key. If you only need your agent to work with your platform account, use the standard setup above.
L325: 
L326: If you’re a [Connect platform](https://docs.stripe.com/connect.md), you can also use MCP to retrieve or update resources for your connected accounts. For example, a support agent could retrieve a customer or investigate a payment for a specific connected account.
L327: MCP doesn’t support OAuth when acting on behalf of connected accounts. Instead, authenticate with a [restricted API key](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys.md#create-a-restricted-api-key) for your platform and grant only the connected-account permissions that your agent needs.
L328: 
L329: To make an MCP call as a connected account, pass the `Stripe-Account` header. This is useful when you provide an agent that allows your connected accounts to make MCP calls through your platform.
L330: ```json
L331: {
L332:   "mcpServers": {
L333:     "stripe": {
L334:       "url": "https://mcp.stripe.com",
L335:       "headers": {
L336:          "Authorization": "Bearer rk_.....",
L337:          "Stripe-Account": "acct_xxxxxxxxx"
L338:       }
L339:     }
L340:   }
L341: }
L342: ```
